posts.title: [MOC] The SMARTER TIE Advanced x2 - Fixing LEGO SMART Play 75421 Darth Vader's TIE Fighter
posts.text: At the time of writing, LEGO 75421 Darth Vader’s TIE Fighter is the cheapest LEGO Star Wars set that includes a SMART Brick, making it a good donor set if you want to try out the SMART Play system. The original set captures Darth Vader’s iconic TIE Advanced x1 from A New Hope, but I felt the exterior could be improved. The gaps around the black Technic beams and the exposed SMART Brick made the model look a little unfinished, so I set out to clean up the design without losing any of the interactive features. For this alternate history build, I imagined what Vader’s next generation starfighter might look like. The TIE Advanced x2 keeps the familiar shape of his personal fighter but replaces the original wings with TIE Interceptor style solar arrays, giving it a sharper and more aggressive profile. I also removed the black Technic beams around the hyperdrive module to close up the gaps and plated over the SMART Brick for a cleaner finish. To make room for the upgraded starfighter, I also scaled down the Rebel base and fuel station side builds, reusing some of their pieces for the TIE Advanced x2. Despite these changes, all the SMART Play functionality is retained, including the interactive lights and sounds. You can still press down on the red lever to activate the play function, and the solid central core makes the fighter comfortable to hold around the hyperdrive module when swooshing it through space. One thing to keep in mind when handling the model is that the tips of the solar arrays are connected by a single stud, so a little care is needed there. The idea was to make Vader’s fighter look better on display while keeping it sturdy and fun to play with. After all, even the Dark Lord of the Sith needs a starfighter that can handle a dogfight! This is my take on how Darth Vader’s personal starfighter could have evolved in an alternate Star Wars history. I hope you enjoy building it as much as I enjoyed designing it! Instructions are on Rebrickable and OpenStuds: https://reb.li/m/281092

posts.title: Lego Blockly: Graphical Common Programming Environment Web App (Using Intuitive Blockly) for All Lego Robotic Platforms.
posts.text: My pleasure. It all works brilliantly!!! I renamed the hubs—works. The appended number is absolutely fine! When the last character is a letter, the number is appended without an underscore; when it is a number, an underscore, and the number are appended. That is PERFECT! I saved the program, closed LEGO Blockly, shut down the hubs (in my example below the handset "TC9750", the City hub in the locomotive "EMD_FP7", and the City hub in the locomotive "Crocodile"), and even rebooted my laptop. After rebooting Windows, I started LEGO Blockly connected the three PUp devices (in arbitrary order, checked that) loaded my program into LEGO Blockly—and: PERFECT! Every hub is correctly showing up in the program. Below is the LEGO Blockly program I am using to control two of my locomotives using one PUp remote. Keys on the left dial = EMD_F7, key on the right dial = Crocodile. "+" increments speed (not power!) by 5 (scale = 100, max. value = 90, as I like to have some power "reserve" for holding the speed constant at max. speed), "-" decrements speed, red button stops the locomotive. The green button is currently used to switch on/off the head/cabin light in the F7. The program is organized as variable setup (I believe this is not even required, as the variables may initialize to 0/false ... depending on type) starting the parallel tasks 1 to 3. Task 1 monitors the left dial keys and sets a new speed value if there is a change; Task 2 does the same thing for the right dial keys. Task 3 is just for displaying the current speed value for both locomotives. That's it :D The screen looks nice and clean . It executes in >no time< ("Program finished"), as the tasks continue to run in the background, so >much< more complex stuff may be added (“in a main loop”, etc.) The setup function and the tasks 1+2 are "collapsed"; task 3 is not, as I want to see the current speed setting (just for fun). This is how it looks like when all blocks are expanded: It is so intuitive and thus so easy to get this going. If I had to run this on an ESP32 - it would be much, much more complicated and elaborate. Fixing the endless errors after failed compilations ... OK, that is my fault, but it always happens to me. It hardly ever happens in LEGO Blockly. Conclusion: LEGO Blockly has become my favorite programming language when playing with electronic LEGO devices. I mean, I can just connect an Interface A (from 1986), add a couple of blocks to the program above. And then use its outputs to switch on/off lamps or whatever vintage stuff comes to mind, and at the same time, the program controls the most recent LEGO PoweredUp stuff (from 2018 onwards). Which is apparently soon phasing out and thus becomes semi-vintage as well . I don't care, though; I have LEGO Blockly. Thank you so much again, Yves! All the best, Thorsten P.S.: When leaving LEGO Blockly, or disconnecting all devices, I usually turn off the handset manually by pressing the green key until the LEED stops blinking. And then I do the LEGO Blockly disconnect. Reason: When disconnecting all three hubs, the handset will find one of the City hubs and connect to it, as they are all ready to connect for a couple of seconds. So you have to shut down the remote manually anyway :D I sometimes forget about that behavior; both stay connected, and then the batteries just drain for nothing ...

posts.title: Using Claude AI for new ports and translations
posts.text: @Toastie can you check it is fixed? Claude answer: Hi Toastie, thanks a lot for the detailed feedback, it's really useful. 1) Emergency Stop and the "(1)": you're right, it's a bug. The outputs really are switched off, but the TC Controller panel isn't redrawn when Emergency Stop (or Reset) is pressed, so it keeps showing the old value. I'll fix it so the panel clears at the same time. 2) What happens when the TC Controller opens: the panel appears, yes. As far as I can see in the code, the Pascal primitives don't come from opening the panel but from the line `uses LTCC;` (or `LTCC2;` for port 926) in the program itself. So the two are independent: a program can use the primitives with the panel closed, and the panel works without any program. Could you check whether the primitives really appear in your Pascal when you only open the panel, without that line? Maybe the example you loaded already contained `uses LTCC;`, but I may also have missed another trigger. 3) Seeing the interface and the controller together: I agree it's awkward on a laptop, as the controller opens below the interface and one of them scrolls out of view. I like your idea: while the TC Controller is open, it takes the Command Center's place right under the Interface A panel, and when you close it the Command Center comes back. The only downside is that you can't type a command and use the controller at the same time, but I don't think anyone really does that. I'll try it and let you know. Thanks again! Claude

posts.text: I wonder what it’ll take for me to jump off this theme entirely. Hobbies-wise it’s been a staple of my life since I was a kid so there’s always been a deep attachment to it. Does anyone else feel that Lego Star Wars as a collecting medium is still the most appealing out there, but as a manner of capturing the soul of Star Wars it’s also the most poorly managed? I’ll always prefer Lego sets to action figures, statues, and the like, but most collectible companies like Hasbro / Hot Toys / Jazwares run orbit-sized circles around Lego when it comes to being able to cover Star Wars content old and new. Maybe that says more about my attachment to Lego in general than it does for Lego Star Wars. On a more positive note, I wonder what the odds are of the McQuarrie figure stands having little cardbacks with backgrounds representing some of his location-based art. Probably not going to happen, but it’d be nice to see those again after how the minifigure polybags used to have them and given the nature of these anniversary figures being concept-art related, it would be very fitting.

posts.title: [MOC] The Crooked Quarter: Victorian Gothic Fantasy District
posts.text: Hello everyone! 👋 I’d like to share my latest creation with you: The Crooked Quarter, an original 11,237-piece LEGO MOC inspired by Victorian Gothic architecture and dark fantasy. Designed it entirely with BrickLink Studio over roughly three weeks. The model depicts a forgotten trading district that mysteriously vanished from official city maps. The quarter features five peculiar shops, each with its own character and story: Calloway’s Cursed Curiosities: A collection of strange antiques and questionable relics. Fiona’s Fabled Flames: Enchanted flames with a touch of danger. Belladonna’s Blessings: Mysterious remedies and rather unusual potions. Grimm & Keys: Locks, keys and secrets waiting to be discovered. Blackveil & Co.: A long-abandoned storefront where things may not be quite as they seem. The buildings feature crooked rooftops, winding staircases, hidden passageways and up to three fully detailed floors. I wanted every shop to feel unique while maintaining a cohesive architectural style throughout the district. One of my main goals was to create a world that feels alive, with plenty of small details to discover both inside and out. I’ve included several exterior views, a few interior highlights and an exploded view to give you a closer look at the design. I’d love to hear your thoughts and feedback, especially on the architecture and detailing! Happy building! 🧱

posts.title: Cannon Cove, Lego 6266: A Fresh Review
posts.text: I recently pieced together a pirate version of Cannon Cove that I will eventually position close to Rock Island Refuge or Forbidden Island when I rebuild my larger pirate base of operations. I think this will go nicely with either of those two, especially Rock Island Refuge, which I envision to be a dilapidated and abandoned imperial fort. This is a nice extension of it. Where I didn't have a suitable original style piece I simply swapped for what was available. This arched window is a good example: I do have a few of the BURP pieces but I'm saving those for a bigger project in my display, so I sort of threw together a few brick-built rocks and another arched window for this side: You've got Burried Treasure in the foreground and to the left we have everyone's favorite pirate captain enjoying a much needed break from the pillaging and plundering that typically fills his days. This is actually from the Pirates of Barnacle Bay and if you recall it is actually Ironhook who comes with this build. These sets, all placed on a Forbidden Island printed baseplate, are a temporary "throw together" until I can craft a more permanent pirate hideout. And of course, the pirate version of Cannon Cove will be a part of that. These additional shanties will probably also find their way into it. For now the Cannon Cove build is the focus and this dark version of it underscores the simplicity and epic interchangeability of these old vintage sets.

posts.title: Anyone have a business use endorsement on their personal policy?
posts.text: Was talking to another insurance agent and he seems to think the business use endorsement policy will be denied if i get into an accident. The truck tows a landscape trailer with mowers on it. The landscape trailer is fully insured and on its own commercial policy. Im just solo. The full commercial auto is like $3k/ year and the personal auto with the business endorsement is like $1300/year. Opinions?

posts.title: What are you running for quote follow-ups and missed calls?
posts.text: hey folks, curious what the room is running these days. im using tradestash for job tracking right now and no complaints there, keeps my crm, quotes, invoices and schedule in one spot which is a big step up from the sticky-note-on-the-dash setup i had before. where im still losing money is two spots it doesnt really cover: follow ups and dealing with missed calls when im on a job. miss two or three a day at times easy and i figure half of those just go call the next guy on the list. what... What are you running for quote follow-ups and missed calls?

posts.title: Heard about a contractor who lost a lot of money over an expired license. How do you prevent this?
posts.text: Heard a story recently that I can't get out of my head. A contractor sent his crew to a job site. GC checked credentials. One guy's license had lapsed. Whole crew got sent home. Lost a lot of money in one day. Got me thinking about my own situation. How does everyone here actually track license and cert renewals for their crew? Especially when you have multiple guys with different certs expiring at different times? Spreadsheet? Calendar reminders? Something else?
